sites.name: See of Rome
sites.summary: Christians were in Rome by the 40s (Suetonius' riots 'at the instigation of Chrestus' under Claudius), Paul wrote to them c. 57, and Nero blamed them for the fire of 64. The letter 1 Clement (c. 96) speaks for the Roman church; Irenaeus later lists Linus, Anacletus and Clement as Peter's successors. A single ruling bishop is secure only from Anicetus (c. 155) or later. By the 4th century the bishop was a great landowner and, from Leo I, claimed primacy over all churches.

sites.name: See of Antioch
sites.summary: Where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11.26) and the base of Paul's missions. Ignatius, the first bishop known from his own writings, was taken to Rome under Trajan to die in the arena and wrote seven letters on the way insisting on obedience to one bishop. Eusebius makes Evodius his predecessor. Paul of Samosata was deposed here in 268. At Chalcedon (451) Antioch ranked third among the patriarchates.

sites.name: See of Alexandria
sites.summary: Eusebius' list from Mark's successor Annianus is legendary; the first historically secure bishop is Demetrius (189-232), who first sponsored then expelled Origen. By Nicaea (canon 6) the bishop ruled all the bishops of Egypt and Libya, and the 'pope' of Alexandria, from Athanasius to Cyril and Dioscorus, was the most powerful churchman in the East until Chalcedon split the Egyptian church.

sites.name: See of Jerusalem
sites.summary: The Jerusalem church was led by James, 'the Lord's brother', whom Paul met there and who presided at the apostolic council (c. 49); Josephus records his stoning in 62. After Hadrian's refoundation as Aelia Capitolina (135) the first gentile bishop was Mark. Subordinate to Caesarea until Juvenal won patriarchal rank at Chalcedon in 451.

sites.name: See of Carthage
sites.summary: Africa's primatial see. The Passion of Perpetua (203) names Bishop Optatus; Agrippinus held a council on rebaptism c. 220; Cyprian (248-258) left the richest archive of a 3rd-century bishop and was beheaded in 258. From 311 the see was split between Catholics (Caecilian) and Donatists (Majorinus, then Donatus).

sites.name: See of Lyon
sites.summary: The church of Lyon and Vienne, Greek-speaking and linked to Asia Minor, sent a letter describing the pogrom of 177, in which the 90-year-old bishop Pothinus died in prison. His successor Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies here, the first systematic attack on Gnosticism.

sites.name: See of Vienne
sites.summary: Co-author with Lyon of the letter on the martyrs of 177, but its first named bishop is Verus at Arles in 314. Vienne later fought Arles for metropolitan rank in Narbonensis.

sites.name: See of Smyrna
sites.summary: Ignatius wrote to Bishop Polycarp c. 110. Polycarp, who claimed to have known the apostle John, visited Anicetus in Rome over the date of Easter and was burned in the stadium c. 155-156 at 86 years old; the Martyrdom of Polycarp is the earliest martyr act.

sites.name: See of Ephesus
sites.summary: Paul's base for over two years and a centre of Johannine tradition. Ignatius praises its bishop Onesimus. Polycrates of Ephesus defended the Asian (Quartodeciman) Easter date against Victor of Rome c. 190. Host of the councils of 431 and 449.

sites.name: See of Magnesia on the Maeander
sites.summary: Ignatius' letter to the Magnesians names their young bishop Damas and urges them not to despise his youth.

sites.name: See of Tralles
sites.summary: Ignatius' letter to the Trallians names Bishop Polybius, who visited him at Smyrna.

sites.name: See of Philadelphia (Lydia)
sites.summary: One of the seven churches of Revelation. Ignatius, who passed through, praises its silent but authoritative bishop without naming him.

sites.name: See of Hierapolis in Phrygia
sites.summary: Papias (c. 120-130) collected oral traditions about the apostles, including the earliest statements on how Mark and Matthew were written. The tomb of the apostle Philip, venerated here, was found in 2011. Apollinaris, bishop c. 170, wrote an apology to Marcus Aurelius.

sites.name: See of Sardis
sites.summary: Melito, bishop c. 170, wrote an Apology to Marcus Aurelius and the homily On the Pascha, with its notorious charge of deicide against Israel, in a city where the synagogue was larger than any church.

sites.name: See of Laodicea on the Lycus
sites.summary: Bishop Sagaris was martyred c. 166 under the proconsul Servilius Paulus, Melito says. The Council of Laodicea (c. 363) issued canons on clergy and the biblical canon.

sites.name: See of Corinth
sites.summary: Paul's church of the letters to the Corinthians; 1 Clement (c. 96) rebukes it for deposing its presbyters. Bishop Dionysius (c. 170) wrote letters to Rome, Athens, Crete and Pontus, the first collected letters of a bishop.

sites.name: See of Athens
sites.summary: Dionysius of Corinth reports that Bishop Publius was martyred and Quadratus revived the church. Athens remained a pagan intellectual centre until Justinian's ban of 529.

sites.name: See of Gortyn
sites.summary: Metropolis of Crete; Dionysius of Corinth praised its bishop Philip, who wrote against Marcion.

sites.name: See of Knossos
sites.summary: Pinytus of Knossos replied to Dionysius of Corinth, urging solid teaching rather than milk; Eusebius admired his letter.

sites.name: See of Sinope
sites.summary: Hippolytus and Epiphanius say Marcion, the shipowner who founded a rival church c. 144, was the son of the bishop of Sinope, who excommunicated him for seducing a virgin (probably a metaphor for corrupting the church).

sites.name: See of Amastris
sites.summary: Dionysius of Corinth wrote to the churches of Pontus at Amastris under Bishop Palmas, who later presided over the Pontic synod on Easter c. 190.

sites.name: See of Anchialus
sites.summary: Thracian port whose bishop Sotas tried to exorcise the Montanist prophetess Priscilla, according to an anti-Montanist source in Eusebius.

sites.name: See of Caesarea Maritima
sites.summary: Metropolitan see of Palestine. Theophilus presided over a synod on Easter c. 190. Origen settled here in 231 and founded the school and library that Pamphilus expanded and Eusebius, bishop c. 313-339, used for his Ecclesiastical History.

sites.name: See of Tyre
sites.summary: Cassius of Tyre joined the Palestinian synod on Easter c. 190. Eusebius preached at the dedication of Paulinus' new basilica at Tyre c. 315, describing it in detail. Origen was buried at Tyre.

sites.name: See of Ptolemais (Acre)
sites.summary: Clarus of Ptolemais joined Theophilus of Caesarea and Cassius of Tyre in the Easter synod of c. 190.

sites.name: See of Edessa
sites.summary: Centre of Syriac Christianity. The legend of King Abgar's letter to Jesus was known to Eusebius. The Chronicle of Edessa records 'the temple of the church of the Christians' destroyed by flood in 201; Palut, said to have been consecrated by Serapion of Antioch, is the first named bishop. Rabbula (412-435) and the School of the Persians made it the hub of Syriac theology.

sites.name: See of Arles
sites.summary: Cyprian urged Pope Stephen to depose Marcianus of Arles c. 254 for his Novatianist rigorism. Marinus of Arles hosted Constantine's council of 314. In the 5th century the see claimed primacy over Gaul, and Caesarius (502-542) ran a model episcopal city.

sites.name: See of Lambaesis
sites.summary: Legionary base of III Augusta. Its bishop Privatus was condemned for heresy by a synod of 90 bishops c. 240, as Cyprian reports.

sites.name: See of Neocaesarea
sites.summary: Gregory the Wonderworker, a pupil of Origen, became bishop c. 240; Gregory of Nyssa's later Life claims he found 17 Christians on arrival and left 17 pagans at his death. His Canonical Letter deals with Christians who collaborated with Gothic raiders in the 250s.

sites.name: See of Caesarea in Cappadocia
sites.summary: Firmilian (c. 232-268) hosted Origen, sided with Cyprian against Rome on rebaptism, and presided at the first synod against Paul of Samosata. Basil (370-379) made the see the leader of Nicene orthodoxy in the East and built the Basileias poorhouse-hospital.

sites.name: See of Iconium
sites.summary: Bishop Celsus invited Origen, a layman, to preach, as Alexander of Jerusalem reminded Demetrius of Alexandria. A synod at Iconium c. 230 rejected heretical baptism.

sites.name: See of Bostra
sites.summary: Beryllus of Bostra taught that Christ had no divinity of his own before the incarnation; Origen was called in and argued him round at a synod c. 244.

sites.name: See of Arsinoe (Fayum)
sites.summary: Bishop Nepos wrote a millenarian Refutation of the Allegorists; Dionysius of Alexandria spent three days debating his followers in the Fayum villages c. 255 and persuaded them.

sites.name: See of Tarsus
sites.summary: Paul's home town. Helenus of Tarsus was one of the leading bishops whom Dionysius of Alexandria lists c. 251 and presided at the synods against Paul of Samosata.

sites.name: See of Legio and Asturica
sites.summary: Cyprian's council of 254 upheld the deposition of Basilides, who had obtained a certificate of sacrifice in the Decian persecution, the earliest evidence for organised churches in Hispania.

sites.name: See of Emerita
sites.summary: Martialis of Emerita was deposed with Basilides for apostasy in 254; Cyprian adds that he belonged to a pagan funerary college. Later the metropolis of Lusitania and the shrine of Eulalia.

sites.name: See of Tolosa
sites.summary: Saturninus was dragged to death by a bull after refusing to sacrifice, according to a 5th-century Passion that dates his mission to c. 250. Gregory of Tours lists him among seven bishops sent to Gaul under Decius.

sites.name: See of Lutetia (Paris)
sites.summary: Gregory of Tours places Dionysius' mission and martyrdom c. 250; the first solidly attested activity is a council at Paris in 360/361. Genovefa built the first basilica over his tomb c. 475.

sites.name: See of Hippo Regius
sites.summary: Theogenes of Hippo voted at Cyprian's council on baptism in 256. Augustine was ordained priest here in 391 against his will and was bishop from 395/6 until he died during the Vandal siege in 430.

sites.name: See of Cirta
sites.summary: Crescens of Cirta voted in 256. The minutes of the 303 confiscation of church property at Cirta, read at a trial of 320, list the bishop's chalices, tunics and stores of clothing, and reveal Bishop Silvanus as a traditor.

sites.name: See of Hadrumetum
sites.summary: Polycarpus of Hadrumetum voted at the council of 256. The town's catacombs hold around 15,000 burials.

sites.name: See of Thamugadi
sites.summary: Novatus of Thamugadi voted in 256. Under Optatus (c. 388-398), ally of the rebel Gildo, Timgad was a Donatist stronghold with one of the largest churches in Africa.

sites.name: See of Tarraco
sites.summary: Bishop Fructuosus was burned alive in the amphitheatre on 21 January 259 with his deacons Augurius and Eulogius, under Valerian's edict. A 6th-century basilica was built in the arena.

sites.name: See of Laodicea ad Mare
sites.summary: Eusebius, an Alexandrian deacon, and then Anatolius, the mathematician who devised a 19-year Easter cycle, were successive bishops of Laodicea after escaping the siege of the Alexandrian Bruchion c. 262.

sites.name: See of Corduba
sites.summary: Ossius (c. 295-357), the most influential Western bishop of his age, attended Elvira, advised Constantine from 312, carried his letter to Alexandria in 324, probably presided at Nicaea, and at nearly 100 was forced to sign the Arian formula of Sirmium in 357.

sites.name: See of Nicomedia
sites.summary: Diocletian's capital, where the Great Persecution began with the destruction of the church on 23 February 303. Bishop Anthimus was beheaded. Eusebius of Nicomedia, Arius' patron, baptised Constantine here in 337.

sites.name: See of Heraclea (Perinthus)
sites.summary: Metropolis of Thrace whose bishop Philippus was burned at Hadrianopolis in 304; Heraclea's bishop originally consecrated the bishop of Byzantium.

sites.name: See of Sirmium
sites.summary: Bishop Irenaeus was beheaded on 6 April 304. Imperial residence and site of four councils in 351-358 that produced the creeds of the Homoian party, including the 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' (357).

sites.name: See of Poetovio
sites.summary: Victorinus of Poetovio, martyred probably in 304, wrote the oldest surviving Latin commentary on the Apocalypse, with millenarian views Jerome toned down.

sites.name: See of Salona
sites.summary: Metropolis of Dalmatia; Bishop Domnius was martyred under Diocletian, whose palace was 5 km away. The great martyr cemeteries of Manastirine and Marusinac lie outside the walls.

sites.name: See of Iliberris (Elvira)
sites.summary: Host city of the synod of Elvira (c. 305), whose 81 canons, signed by 19 bishops, ban pictures in churches, marriages with pagans and Jews, and clerical sex.

sites.name: See of Toletum
sites.summary: Melantius of Toledo attended Elvira. In the Visigothic kingdom Toledo became the royal see, host of the councils from 400 and of the Third Council (589) at which Reccared converted.

sites.name: See of Thmuis
sites.summary: Phileas, a rich and learned bishop, wrote from prison describing the tortures in Alexandria and was beheaded c. 306; his trial transcript survives on papyrus (P. Bodmer XX).

sites.name: See of Lycopolis
sites.summary: Meletius of Lycopolis ordained clergy in other sees during the persecution, starting the Melitian schism that Nicaea tried to settle and that lasted into the 8th century.

sites.name: See of Siscia
sites.summary: Bishop Quirinus was drowned in the river at Savaria in 309 with a millstone around his neck, according to Jerome's Chronicle and his Passion.

sites.name: See of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
sites.summary: Papa bar Aggai (c. 310-329) asserted the primacy of the Sasanian capital over Persian bishops. Simeon bar Sabba'e was executed by Shapur II in 344. The Synod of Isaac (410) organised the Church of the East under a catholicos.

sites.name: See of Gaza
sites.summary: Silvanus, 'bishop of the churches around Gaza', was beheaded at the Phaeno mines in 311. Gaza remained largely pagan until Porphyry (395-420) won imperial orders to destroy the Marneion in 402.

sites.name: See of Emesa
sites.summary: Silvanus of Emesa was thrown to the beasts in 312, after 40 years as bishop, Eusebius says.

sites.name: See of Mediolanum
sites.summary: Merocles sat at the Roman synod of 313 and at Arles in 314. As imperial residence Milan became a leading see; Ambrose (374-397) baptised Augustine in 387 and forced Theodosius I into penance in 390.

sites.name: See of Capua
sites.summary: Proterius of Capua sat at Miltiades' synod of 313 on the Donatist case and was at Arles in 314.

sites.name: See of Ostia
sites.summary: Maximus of Ostia sat at the Roman synod of 313; by custom the bishop of Ostia consecrated the bishop of Rome. Augustine's mother Monica died at Ostia in 387.

sites.name: See of Florentia
sites.summary: Felix of Florentia sat at the Roman synod of 313 under Miltiades, the first attested bishop in Etruria.

sites.name: See of Ariminum
sites.summary: Stennius of Ariminum sat at the synod of 313. In 359 over 400 Western bishops met at Ariminum and were pressured into a Homoian creed.

sites.name: See of Beneventum
sites.summary: Theophilus of Beneventum sat at Miltiades' synod of 313, per Optatus' list of the Italian bishops.

sites.name: See of Augustodunum
sites.summary: Reticius of Autun, with Maternus and Marinus, was one of three Gallic bishops Constantine sent to judge the Donatists in Rome in 313. Jerome knew his commentary on the Song of Songs.

sites.name: See of Colonia Agrippina
sites.summary: Maternus of Cologne sat at Rome in 313 and Arles in 314; a 4th-century Christian community is attested by burials and the predecessor of St Gereon.

sites.name: See of Augusta Treverorum
sites.summary: Agricius attended Arles in 314. As imperial capital Trier hosted Athanasius in exile (335-337) and Priscillian's trial and execution (385).

sites.name: See of Londinium
sites.summary: Restitutus of London attended the Council of Arles in 314 with the bishops of York and probably Lincoln, a priest and a deacon: the first firm evidence of an organised British church.

sites.name: See of Eboracum
sites.summary: Eborius of York attended Arles in 314. At Ariminum in 359 three British bishops were so poor they accepted the imperial travel allowance the others refused, says Sulpicius Severus.

sites.name: See of Lindum (probably)
sites.summary: The Arles list has Adelfius 'from the city of the colony of the Londoners', usually emended to Lindum (Lincoln), possibly Camulodunum.

sites.name: See of Durocortorum
sites.summary: Imbetausius of Reims attended Arles in 314. Remigius of Reims baptised Clovis, by tradition at Christmas c. 496-508.

sites.name: See of Rotomagus
sites.summary: Avitianus of Rouen attended Arles in 314. Victricius (c. 386-407) wrote In Praise of the Saints on the relics he received.

sites.name: See of Burdigala
sites.summary: Orientalis of Bordeaux attended Arles in 314. A synod at Bordeaux in 384 condemned Priscillian, who appealed to the usurper Maximus.

sites.name: See of Massalia
sites.summary: Oresius of Marseille attended Arles in 314. John Cassian founded St Victor here c. 415.

sites.name: See of Vasio
sites.summary: Daphnus of Vaison attended Arles in 314; Vaison hosted councils in 442 and 529.

sites.name: See of Syracuse
sites.summary: Constantine's letter summoning Chrestus to Arles, with travel by public post, is quoted by Eusebius. The catacombs of San Giovanni are the largest outside Rome.

sites.name: See of Carales
sites.summary: Quintasius of Carales attended Arles in 314. Lucifer of Cagliari (d. 370), exiled for defending Athanasius, founded a rigorist schism.

sites.name: See of Aquileia
sites.summary: Theodore attended Arles in 314 and built the double basilica with its mosaic floor. Ambrose's council of Aquileia (381) deposed the Homoian bishops Palladius and Secundianus.

sites.name: See of Caesaraugusta
sites.summary: Valerius of Caesaraugusta attended Arles in 314; Cyprian's letter of 254 already praises a Felix of the city. A council here in 380 condemned Priscillian's practices.

sites.name: See of Ancyra
sites.summary: Host of the council of 314 on the lapsed. Marcellus of Ancyra, an extreme anti-Arian at Nicaea, was deposed in 336 for Sabellianism; the creed clause 'his kingdom will have no end' was added against him.

sites.name: See of Amaseia
sites.summary: Basileus of Amaseia attended Ancyra (314) and was executed under Licinius c. 322, an episode Eusebius cites as Licinius' persecution.

sites.name: See of Byzantium/Constantinople
sites.summary: A minor suffragan of Heraclea until Constantine's refoundation; Alexander (c. 314-337) prayed that Arius, due to be readmitted to communion in 336, should not be; Arius died suddenly the day before. The council of 381 gave its bishop second rank after Rome, and canon 28 of Chalcedon (451) equal privileges, which Rome rejected.

sites.name: See of Nicaea
sites.summary: Theognis of Nicaea signed the creed of 325 but not the anathemas and was exiled with Eusebius of Nicomedia, then recalled c. 328.

sites.name: See of Chalcedon
sites.summary: Maris of Chalcedon, an Arian sympathiser, attended Nicaea; old and blind, he later rebuked Julian to his face as an apostate. The council of 451 met in the martyrium of St Euphemia here.

sites.name: See of Nisibis
sites.summary: Jacob of Nisibis attended Nicaea; legend credits his prayers with saving the city in Shapur II's sieges. Ephrem the Syrian served him and his successors until Nisibis was ceded to Persia in 363.

sites.name: See of Damascus
sites.summary: Magnus of Damascus signed at Nicaea. The city's church of John the Baptist, built in the old temple of Jupiter under Theodosius, became the Umayyad mosque.

sites.name: See of Thessalonica
sites.summary: Paul's church of the Thessalonian letters; its first named bishop, Alexander, signed at Nicaea. From the late 4th century the bishop was papal vicar for Illyricum. Theodosius' massacre in the hippodrome (390) led to his penance before Ambrose.

sites.name: See of Serdica
sites.summary: Protogenes of Serdica signed at Nicaea and hosted the council of 343, which split into Western and Eastern assemblies excommunicating each other.

sites.name: See of Stobi
sites.summary: Budius of Stobi signed at Nicaea for Macedonia; the city's episcopal basilica had several rebuildings in the 4th-6th centuries.

sites.name: See of Larissa
sites.summary: Achillius of Larissa, metropolitan of Thessaly, signed at Nicaea.

sites.name: See of Trimithus (Cyprus)
sites.summary: Spyridon, a shepherd-bishop and Nicaea participant according to Rufinus and Socrates, became Cyprus' best known saint; his relics are now on Corfu. Epiphanius of Salamis (367-403) was the island's great metropolitan.

sites.name: See of Ptolemais (Pentapolis)
sites.summary: Secundus of Ptolemais refused to sign at Nicaea and was exiled with Arius. Synesius, a Neoplatonist who refused to give up his wife, was bishop from 410 and wrote on the nomad raids.

sites.name: See of the Bosporus
sites.summary: Domnus of Bosporus signed at Nicaea, the first bishop on the north shore of the Black Sea.

sites.name: See of Pityus
sites.summary: Stratophilus of Pityus, a frontier fort in Colchis, signed at Nicaea; John Chrysostom died on the way to exile there in 407.

sites.name: See of Aksum
sites.summary: Frumentius, a Tyrian shipwrecked as a boy and raised at the Aksumite court, was consecrated bishop by Athanasius c. 330-340; King Ezana's coins switch from pagan symbols to the cross. Constantius II wrote to the Aksumite kings demanding Frumentius' recall.

sites.name: See of Hadrianopolis
sites.summary: Eutropius of Hadrianopolis, an anti-Arian, was deposed c. 331 after Eusebius of Nicomedia's party accused him before Constantine's half-sister Basilina.

sites.name: See of Mursa
sites.summary: Valens of Mursa, with Ursacius the leader of Western Homoians, told Constantius II of his victory over Magnentius at Mursa (351) before the messengers arrived, claiming an angel had told him.

sites.name: See of Singidunum
sites.summary: Ursacius of Singidunum, a pupil of Arius, was a leading Homoian at Tyre (335), Sirmium and Ariminum.

sites.name: See of Caesarodunum (Tours)
sites.summary: Gregory of Tours, himself bishop from 573, lists Gatianus and then Litorius (c. 337) before Martin, the soldier-monk made bishop in 371, whose tomb made Tours the chief pilgrimage centre of Gaul.

sites.name: See of Ravenna
sites.summary: Severus signed at Serdica in 343. When Honorius moved the court to Ravenna in 402 the see rose rapidly: Peter Chrysologus, Neon's baptistery, and under Justinian the archbishops Maximian and Agnellus.

sites.name: See of Atuatuca Tungrorum
sites.summary: Servatius signed at Serdica (343) and attended Ariminum (359), the northernmost bishop on the continent; his see later moved to Maastricht, where his tomb became a cult centre.

sites.name: See of Philippi
sites.summary: Paul's first European church, to which Polycarp wrote c. 120 addressing presbyters, not a bishop. Porphyrius of Philippi is listed at Serdica. The octagonal church and great basilicas of the 5th-6th centuries dominate the site.

sites.name: See of Verona
sites.summary: Zeno of Verona (c. 362-372), probably an African, left 93 sermons. Verona later became a Gothic and Lombard royal city.

sites.name: See of Tomis
sites.summary: Bretanion of Tomis, the only bishop of Scythia, defied Valens to his face c. 368, according to Sozomen. Theotimus (c. 400) evangelised the Goths across the Danube.

sites.name: See of Octodurus
sites.summary: Theodore of Octodurus attended Ambrose's council of Aquileia in 381 and promoted the cult of the Theban Legion at Agaune; his see later moved to Sion.

sites.name: See of Avila
sites.summary: Priscillian, a lay ascetic made bishop of Ávila c. 381, was tried for sorcery before the usurper Maximus and beheaded at Trier in 385 with six followers, the first Christians executed for heresy by a Christian ruler; Martin of Tours and Ambrose protested.

sites.name: See of Bracara
sites.summary: Paternus of Braga renounced Priscillianism at the First Council of Toledo in 400. Under the Sueves Braga became a royal see; Martin of Braga converted them to Catholicism c. 560.

sites.name: See of Cyrrhus
sites.summary: Theodoret (423-c. 460) governed 800 parishes, wrote an Ecclesiastical History and the Religious History of Syrian ascetics, was deposed at Ephesus II (449) and restored at Chalcedon.

sites.name: Palladius and the Irish mission
sites.summary: Prosper records that in 431 Pope Celestine sent Palladius as 'first bishop to the Irish believing in Christ'. Patrick's Confessio describes his own mission later in the 5th century; Armagh's claim to be his see is 7th-century propaganda.
